History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
Young woman with no significant past medical history presents via tele-visit with a first episode of severe, diffuse but right-eye–predominant headache lasting 3 days, accompanied by photophobia and transient visual “shooting lights,” partially relieved by ibuprofen; clinician suspects migraine with aura and arranges face-to-face neurological/ fundoscopic examination and stronger analgesia.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “Blinding” headache for 3 days.  
• Onset – Sudden upon waking three days ago.  
• Course – Constant; intensity 8/10 falling to ~5/10 after ibuprofen; has not fully resolved.  
• Location – Generalized, worst over right eye.  
• Character/Associated symptoms  
  – Photophobia (bright light aggravates).  
  – Transient visual disturbance described as “shooting light.”  
  – Mild nausea; no vomiting.  
  – No numbness, tingling, weakness, speech difficulty, smell or taste change.  
  – No fever, sinus pain, nasal congestion, cough, nosebleed.  
• Aggravating factors – Bright light; standing quickly; sudden head movement.  
• Relieving factors – Partial relief with ibuprofen; sleep (headache does not wake her).  
• Impact – Difficulty concentrating; missed portions of work-from-home duties.  
• Previous headaches – Occasional mild <2-day headaches relieved by ibuprofen; none this severe.  
• Review of systems – Negative for weight change; reports low energy likely related to headache. Otherwise unremarkable.

Past Medical History:
• Remote unspecified childhood “pain,” resolved; no diagnosis given.  
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Medications:  
  – Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand not stated), started 1 year ago; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Ibuprofen PRN for headache; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: Denies drug or other allergies.

Social History:
• Lives alone; works from home.  
• Smoking: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: ~3 drinks, once weekly.  
• Recreational drugs: Denies.  
• Recent travel: None.

Family History:
• Mother has migraines with vomiting.  
• No other family conditions noted.

Physical Examination:
(Not performed – video consultation only. No vitals provided.)

Investigations:
• None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – New severe headache with visual symptoms  
• Assessment: Likely migraine with aura; must exclude secondary causes (e.g., cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension).  
• Plan:  
  – Arrange in-person appointment for full neurological exam and fundoscopy.  
  – Prescribe stronger NSAID (specific drug not documented) and advise concurrent paracetamol; take with food.  
  – Safety-net: If headache worsens, changes character, or becomes unbearable before appointment, attend Emergency Department or call service.

Issue 2 – Combined oral contraceptive pill use in context of migraine-type headache  
• Assessment: Estrogen-containing OCP may precipitate migraine with aura; carries thrombotic risk.  
• Plan:  
  – Check blood pressure at upcoming visit.  
  – Re-assess need for alternative contraception if migraines with aura confirmed.

Issue 3 – Symptom control / functional impairment  
• Assessment: Headache affecting work-from-home productivity and energy.  
• Plan:  
  – Initiate stronger NSAID + paracetamol regimen.  
  – Advise rest in dark room, hydration, regular meals.  
  – Provide medical certificate for work adjustments if needed (not explicitly discussed; omit if not provided).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood: unilateral severe pain, photophobia, visual phenomena, family history, partial NSAID response.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Moderate likelihood: female on estrogen OCP, new persistent headache, positional element; no focal deficits but serious diagnosis to exclude.  
3. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – Moderate likelihood: young woman, visual disturbance; needs optic-disc exam. No papilledema reported yet.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements: No vitals, neurological or fundoscopic findings, lab work, or imaging documented; medication doses not recorded; no explicit allergy confirmation beyond “No.”  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; short inaudible segments (patient identifiers, medication brand) but clinical content intact.
